processing: A mixed drink rather than a processed tea: brewed and chilled iced tea combined with lemonade.
harvest_season: No harvest involved: it is made or bought year-round from everyday tea.
appearance_dry: No dry form of its own; home versions usually start from ordinary black tea.
appearance_liquor: Hazy golden amber over ice, cloudy from the lemonade.
appearance_wet: Not applicable: the leaf or bag is removed before mixing.
taste_profile: Sweet and tart together, with lemon up front and tea tannin underneath; more tea makes it drier, a half-and-half mix makes it sweeter.

brewing.notes: Brew strong black tea, chill it, and mix over ice with lemonade. Three parts unsweetened tea to one part lemonade is the ratio credited to Palmer himself; half and half is the sweeter commercial style.

vintage_note: No vintage or season: it is mixed fresh at home or a bar, or sold ready to drink in cans and bottles year-round. AriZona's version carries the licensed Arnold Palmer trademark; Snapple and Nantucket Nectars sell the mix as half-and-half.
description:
An Arnold Palmer is iced tea mixed with lemonade, named after the American golfer who was known for ordering it. It is a drink rather than a tea type, and it also goes by half-and-half.

There is no tea-making trick to it. Brew the tea, chill it, add lemonade. The one real decision is the ratio, and that decides whether you get a tea drink or a lemon drink.

Palmer's own preference is usually given as mostly unsweetened tea, three parts to one. The AriZona canned version advertises half and half, which is much sweeter. Making it strong enough matters, because weak tea disappears behind lemonade and ice.

The bottled versions are easy to find, but home mixing lets you control the sugar. Alcoholic relatives exist too: the John Daly with vodka, and the Lee Trevino or Juan Daly with tequila.
history:
The name is usually traced to the late 1960s. In the 2012 ESPN 30 for 30 short about the drink, Palmer says a woman overheard his order at lunch after a long day designing a golf course in Palm Springs, California, and asked for that Arnold Palmer drink too.

The drink then went commercial: AriZona sells a version under the licensed Arnold Palmer trademark, while Snapple and Nantucket Nectars have sold the same mix under half-and-half names. In early 2018 MillerCoors began distributing a malt-based version called Arnold Palmer Spiked.
